items.title: The halting problem
items.claim: Alan Turing's 1936 paper proved a famous result about algorithms. What did it show?

options.text: No general algorithm can determine in advance whether an arbitrary program halts

items.reveal:
Turing's 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers' established that no algorithm can correctly answer 'does program P halt on input I?' for all P, I.

The proof uses a diagonal argument similar to Cantor's.
items.why: Computing has provable limits, set out before the first electronic computer was built.

items.title: More cores don't automatically mean more speed
items.claim: Single-threaded code on a 16-core CPU runs at what speed compared to a 4-core CPU of the same generation?

options.text: Roughly the same — single-threaded code uses one core. Multi-core helps only if the workload is parallel; Amdahl's law caps speedup by the serial fraction

items.reveal:
Gene Amdahl's 1967 paper argued that if a fraction f of a program is sequential, the maximum speedup from parallelisation is 1/f. If 10% is serial, the limit is 10x even with infinite cores.

Gustafson's law (1988) softens this: for fixed time and growing problem size, you can use more cores productively. Real performance gains since ~2005 (when clock speeds plateaued) have come from cores + SIMD + GPU + algorithmic improvements, not just GHz.
items.why: Headline core counts mislead about real performance. The relevant question is what fraction of your workload can run in parallel.
